learnerStatement: Simulated learner. This review finds problems; it is not evidence that anyone learned.
learnerBoundary: Everyday numeracy, simple charts, comparing numbers and familiar household objects; no domain-specific theory assumed.

observations.prediction: Selected More and locked the purchasing-power prediction for three percent interest and five percent price growth.
observations.exploration: At one percent price growth, purchasing power was up two percent. Set price growth to three percent: exactly unchanged. Set five percent: down 1.9%, with $103 savings compared against a $105 basket.
observations.reveal: The reveal corrected the answer to Less, gave the $98.10 present purchasing power equivalent, and explained the exact 1.03 divided by 1.05 minus one ratio versus the approximate three minus five percent subtraction. It accurately referenced the tested three-percent equality boundary and disclosed one year, one basket and no tax.
observations.visual: Inspected the inline dark 1257 by 936 screenshot at five percent. A common number line placed the savings marker at $103 and basket price at $105, with a negative 1.9% readout. The growing balance and faster-growing cost were directly comparable.
observations.isolation: No-history evaluation preview banner present. Visible trust count ignored.
observations.reference: Own CUA tab 543884175 snapshots and inspected inline screenshot; no screenshot file saved.

prediction.reason: The question separates nominal balance growth from purchasing power.
prediction.evidence: Selected More despite price growth exceeding interest.

interaction.reason: The price slider exposes gain, equality and loss with a clear boundary.
interaction.evidence: One, three and five percent price growth produce positive, zero and negative real changes.

payoff.reason: The reveal explains the exact ratio and its small-rate approximation.
payoff.evidence: It gives 1.03 divided by 1.05 and distinguishes -1.9% from about -2%.

clarity.reason: Two prices on one scale make the comparison explicit.
clarity.evidence: The $103 balance falls short of the $105 basket.

transfer.reason: The general real-rate rule is explained without a fresh application.
transfer.evidence: Only the same savings and basket case is varied.

accessibility.evidence: Keyboard, focus, contrast audit, phone, zoom/reflow and motion unknown.

surprise.reason: An increasing balance can buy less.
surprise.evidence: Three percent interest still leaves a purchasing-power loss at five percent inflation.

visualExplanation.reason: The shared number line makes the shortfall visible.
visualExplanation.evidence: The basket marker lies beyond the savings marker.

playfulness.reason: One slider supports a straightforward boundary search.
playfulness.evidence: The three-percent equality point can be found directly.

practicalValue.reason: It clarifies nominal versus real growth.
practicalValue.evidence: The exact ratio and approximation are both supplied.

depth.reason: The lesson distinguishes approximate subtraction from the exact calculation.
depth.evidence: The final result is -1.9%, not exactly -2%.

complexity.reason: Familiar money and basket costs support the new real-rate distinction.
complexity.conceptualDemand: Low to moderate: compare growth in money with growth in what it buys.
complexity.interfaceBurden: Low: one slider and a five-percent preset.
complexity.conceptualChallenge: A larger nominal amount need not represent more goods.
complexity.prerequisiteNovelty: Real return and ratio adjustment are introduced.
complexity.notationRepresentationBurden: Low to moderate: dollar markers, percentages and one ratio formula.

whyCool: A balance can grow while its buying power shrinks, and two marks on one scale make the contradiction disappear.
caveat: The model fixes one year, one basket and a three-percent interest rate, omitting taxes and changing spending patterns.
missingEvidence: No fresh nominal rate or distinct application was tested.
